blocks.md: **Inside each education group, the variance of log hourly wages rose in the early 1980s. From the mid-1980s it contracted for every group except college graduates: by the 2000s dropouts were below their 1970s level (≈0.12–0.13), while college graduates kept rising to ≈0.30.**
Values read off the lecture chart, approximate.
College graduates dipped to ≈0.21 around 1979 before rising.

- **Variance rises with education** (in the 2000s, the more educated the group, the more dispersed its wages).
- **Composition**: the college share also rose, so total variance can rise even if no group's variance changes — see [Composition Adjustment](note:composition-adjustment) and [US Variance of Log Wages 1973-2009](note:us-variance-of-log-wages-1973-2009).
- **The split pattern fits polarization**: compression inside low-education groups (mostly in the bottom half) and widening inside college groups (mostly in the top half) — see [Wage Polarization](note:wage-polarization).
